extracted.intended_audience: readers of moral/philosophical essays; educated humanists or students of rhetoric, leadership, and education
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for judging clemency, prudence, courage, and scholarly learning; guidance on what constitutes true wisdom versus pedantry and how leaders should comport themselves in the face of conspiracy and fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of clemency
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercy and forgiveness can win lasting loyalty and honor; pardoning a conspirator may convert an enemy into a devoted friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Augustus forgiving Cinna (who later became a friend and heir) versus examples where clemency did not prevent later treason; forgiving is more noble and generous, and though it may miscarry by Fortune, the intention remains commendable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Fortune in success
rubrics_metrics.description: Many arts and great deeds depend significantly on good luck or Fortune, not purely on the practitioner's skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physicians appearing fortunate when a cure 'hits', poets experiencing raptures 'beyond their sufficiency', painters producing touches that surprise themselves, and captains relying on fortunate turns in war. Therefore one should acknowledge chance and not over-attribute success to human art alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: When uncertain, choose the course with greatest appearance of honesty and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: In hard cases where prudence cannot clearly determine the best path, prefer the action that shows the most honesty and justice rather than the supposedly shortest/most expedient route.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral worth attaches to intentions; even if a merciful course fails, it is not blameworthy if chosen for honorable reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against over-circumspect, distrusting prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive suspicion and jealous vigilance are destructive: they invite misery, prevent great and generous exploits, and may worse the ruler's condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples (Dion, Alexander, Louis XI) showing the torment of perpetual suspicion; recommends moderate trust, occasional bold exposure of oneself to inspire reciprocal confidence rather than constant guarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine confidence and undaunted assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader's open, fearless demeanour—real not feigned—secures authority and can command respect and obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feigned resolution with a pale or trembling countenance is ineffective. To gain heart and will of others, submission or entrustment must appear free and without constraint; Caesar's forthrightness is praised as exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish intelligence of conspiracies as deterrent
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes should publicly announce the plots and informations they receive to foster a reputation of good intelligence and to deter further conspiracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dionysius paying a man to boast of a secret kept enemies in awe; publicizing discoveries makes subjects believe the ruler is well informed and thus less likely to be plotted against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create bold, reassuring public displays to defuse danger
rubrics_metrics.description: When suspicion threatens, officers and leaders should show confidence publicly (e.g., ride boldly, encourage volleys) to transform fear into mutual trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recounted muster where officers rode cheerfully through ranks and ordered volleys succeeded in creating wholesome confidence among suspicious troops—practical advice for managing tense public situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: True scholarship: judgement and virtue over mere erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: Real learning should produce improved judgment and moral goodness, not merely a stocked memory of facts and quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes education that 'furnish[es] our heads with knowledge; but not a word of judgment and virtue.' He insists 'We should rather examine, who is better learned, than who is more learned.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry: do not substitute memory for understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedantry is characterized by a full memory but an empty judgment—parroting others' words without original thought or practical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedants 'go picking knowledge... and hold it at the tongue’s end' to display, not to internalize; they are described as coxcombs who know authors' phrases but not the matters at hand. The antidote is to make knowledge truly one's own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should teach integration and use of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A good education must train students to digest and incorporate learning so it nourishes the soul and informs action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of schooling that leaves scholars 'swelled and puffed up with vain and empty shreds'—advocates educating the conscience and understanding alongside memory; 'we must make [knowledge] our own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application matters: usefulness over abstract display
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth of sciences and letters is proved when applied; theoretical mastery without capacity to act is deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Archimedes turning contemplation into engines for defence; Thales applying wisdom to profitable affairs. Montaigne prefers scholars who can perform in public business rather than only muse in abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural wit can rival artificial learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature sometimes produces genuine wit and understanding where art is absent; thus contrived, over-learned expressions are not superior by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites the Gascon proverb and examples of unstudied nations producing strong effects of wit; implies valuation of natural, spontaneous intelligence over forced pedantic display.
